source: Hampton (1996) Conjunctions of visually based categories: overextension and compensation (JEP:LMC 22)
finding: Overextension (item accepted in 'A and B' but rejected from A alone) generalises from word categories (sports/games) to visual stimuli: colored letter shapes and cartoon faces.
numbers: 4 experiments. Exp 1 colored letters: 163 overextensions vs 46 underextensions. Cartoon faces: 239 vs 51. Face sign test over participants: 34 over-extended more, 8 the reverse, z=3.86, p<.001. Overextended more often: letter shape 37% vs color 12%; intelligence 51% vs emotion 13%.
limits: Stimuli were placed near category borders, which adds noise. The author argues pure guessing cannot give more than 3 times as many over- as underextensions; the data exceed that.
agent_relevance: A judge asked 'is X an A-B?' accepts borderline items too easily. Treat conjunction membership as looser than either part.

source: Hampton (1996) JEP:LMC: control for guessing, base rate and response format (Exp 2 and 3)
finding: Overextension survives a change of base rate and a yes/no format, so it is not only a response bias.
numbers: Exp 2: 32 participants per condition. Positive conjunctive categorization letters 27% (standard) vs 26% (augmented); faces 33% vs 39%. Augmenting the share of items in both categories to about 50% raised face double overextensions from 6% to 16%. Exp 3 used yes/no throughout.
limits: Faces' intelligence scale was unreliable (disagreement S=30% vs 13% for happiness).
agent_relevance: Base rate and answer format move how much a judge over-accepts. Fix the format of any scoring step in the agent.

source: Hampton (1996) JEP:LMC: compensation between constituents
finding: Strong typicality in one category can compensate for borderline membership in the other, and the compensation is asymmetric between dimensions.
numbers: Independent-decision intersection predicts 25% positive conjunction when each constituent is at 50%; observed positive conjunctive rates were 26% to 39% depending on set. More overextension for faces than letters.
limits: Compensation was weaker for color than for letter shape.
agent_relevance: Rank candidate merges with a combined score, not a hard threshold on each part.

source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (APA chapter): rates in Hampton 1987
finding: Emergent attributes (true of the conjunction, not of either part) are rare in intersective conjunctions. Most attributes are inherited.
numbers: Under strict scoring only 3 of 174 attributes were emergent; lenient scoring gave 11. Of 37 attributes unimportant for both constituents, about 8% were important for both orderings of the conjunction. 5 conjunctions had none. More emergence for low set overlap (Pets/Birds) than high overlap (Sports/Games).
quote: it must be concluded that there is relatively little evidence for creative emergence
limits: Review by the original author; the 1987 paper itself was not opened. Depends on rating thresholds.
agent_relevance: Most of what merging gives is inheritance plus selection. Emergence is a minority outcome, so do not expect it by default.

source: Hampton (1996) chapter: negated constituents test (Hampton 1989 data)
finding: Using 'A which are not B' removes the logical route to new attributes, so any new attribute is a cleaner emergence test.
numbers: 6 category pairs, 51 attributes with median 0% for head noun A. 24 stayed 0% for 'A which are not B', 11 broke it slightly (median 0-5%, probably noise), only 6 reached 10% or more. Those 6 are mostly category stretching (a tent as a dwelling).
limits: Small count; emergence came from recalling familiar instances of a broadened category, not from inventing.
agent_relevance: Distant-domain seeds may give stretch (broader category) rather than invention. Check whether a 'new' feature is only a broader instance.

source: Hampton (1996) chapter: congruent vs incongruent trait pairs (Hampson 1990)
finding: Congruent trait pairs show full inheritance. Incongruent pairs lose some inherited features. No emergence in either.
numbers: Congruent: complete inheritance for 31 of 32 attributes. Incongruent: 16 of 25 behaviours likely for one constituent were inherited, 9 were not. No emergent attributes in any trait pair.
limits: Second-hand report; traits, not noun-noun compounds.
agent_relevance: When parts conflict, the merge drops features. Expect loss as well as gain.

source: Hampton (1996) chapter: social stereotype conjunctions and point of view (Hampton, Dillane, Oren)
finding: The viewpoint given to the judge changes what a conjunction like 'Socialist Stockbroker' means. The usual pattern is antagonism: the conjunction resembles the 'other' constituent.
numbers: 210 attributes over 4 category pairs; 2 true of both categories. Of 65 positive attributes true of one's own viewpoint, 11 (17%) were inherited. Of 80 true of the other category, 55 (69%) were inherited, 84% of them negative. 63 attributes false of both constituents: 22 (35%) true of the conjunction (emergent). Antagonism in 7 of 8 materials in Exp 1.
limits: Opinions of imaginers, not members. Gender-linked pairs: male viewpoints more antagonistic (rough count 19 negative vs 8 positive emergent for men; 34 positive vs 3 negative for women). Chapter reports no inferential tests here.
agent_relevance: Instruction framing (whose viewpoint) is a big moderator. A persona in the prompt will change the merged concept.

source: Hampton (1996) chapter: imagining impossible combinations
finding: When forced to merge incompatible categories (fruit that is furniture), people resolve incompatibilities by changing one concept, and emergent attributes become common.
numbers: Nine concept pairs; 20 subjects in two order groups of 10 (one dropped). Roughly 220 attributes mainly true of one constituent vs about 170 emergent (informal count by the author). Hardest pair: food flavoring that is a tool. One order group found the task easier; order x pair interaction not significant.
limits: Small N, informal coding, no inter-rater check. Large differences in effort: some gave puns or surface similarity.
agent_relevance: Forcing a merge of distant pairs yields many emergent features, but quality varies by person. One sample is unreliable; code should rank several.

source: Wisniewski and Gentner (1991) On the combinatorial semantics of noun pairs: minor and major adjustments to meaning
finding: Noun-noun meanings are not only slot filling (relation linking). Property mapping and structure mapping also occur, with major changes to the head concept.
numbers: 400 novel noun-noun phrases (200 pairings in both orders); each of 20 subjects defined 20. Two raters agreed on 87% of judgments. Only 40% of descriptions were judged to state a relation. About 30% had the form 'property Y' or 'Y with property' (e.g. 'a large frog' for elephant frog).
limits: Authors' own coding; the copy read is poor OCR, numbers were cross-checked in context. Nouns came from fixed groups (animals, artifacts, mass nouns).
agent_relevance: Merging by relation alone misses most of what people do. Try several modes: relation, property transfer, structure alignment.

source: Wisniewski and Gentner (1991): mass nouns and who keeps reference
finding: Which noun the phrase refers to depends on the pair type. A mass-noun modifier often makes the phrase 'object made of the mass'.
numbers: 59 of 100 mass-count descriptions described an object made of the mass term (27 mass-animal, 32 mass-artifact). Mass-animal: the animal lost reference in 26 of 27 (96%). Mass-artifact: the artifact kept reference in 21 of 32 (66%), when its function was preserved (clay ladder) and lost it when not (candy ladder).
limits: Referent judged by a group of undergraduates; proportions only, no tests.
agent_relevance: Check function preservation when merging: if the head's function breaks, the modifier tends to become the referent.

source: Hampton (2013) Commentary on Pothos and Busemeyer: quantum probability cannot capture the guppy effect (BBS)
finding: Hampton argues a sequential-projection (quantum) model cannot give double overextension because each projection lowers probability, while the composite prototype model can.
numbers: Cites Storms et al. (2005) that the guppy effect (item a better member of A-and-B than of either A or B) is real but much rarer than simple overextension of one conjunct. Example: a ski-lift is more likely a 'machine that is a vehicle' than a vehicle.
quote: much rarer than simple overextension of one conjunct
limits: Short commentary, no new data. Storms et al. not opened.
agent_relevance: Double overextension discriminates intensional (composite prototype) accounts from projection accounts.

source: Aerts, Sozzo, Veloz and colleagues (2016) Context and interference effects in the combinations of natural concepts
finding: A three-dimensional complex Hilbert space model (superposition plus interference) reproduces Hampton's overextension and underextension data for conjunctions and disjunctions.
numbers: Hampton's 7-point membership scale. Refrigerator for House Furnishings/Furniture: mu(A)=0.9, mu(B)=0.7, mu(A or B)=0.575 (double underextension). TV for Furniture/Household Appliances: 0.7, 0.9, mu(A and B)=0.925 (double overextension). Authors state a large part of Hampton's conjunction data cannot be placed in one Kolmogorov probability space.
limits: Per-item fitted interference angle gives the model flexibility, so fit is partly free. Hampton (2013) disputes the projection version of quantum accounts.
agent_relevance: A rival model. Warns against scoring conjunction fit with a simple min rule.

source: Song, Lee, Ahn, Sung and Kim (2025) Is a peeled apple still red? CCPT dataset (arXiv 2502.06086)
finding: LLMs, including o1 and GPT-4o, struggle to generate emergent properties of a combination more than canceled ones. Humans beat LLMs on emergent, LLMs beat humans on canceled.
numbers: CCPT: 12,315 annotated triplets (phrase, property, type), 2,501 emergent. Human majority label accuracy on property type: 87% emergent, 79% component, 76% canceled, 81% overall. GPT-4o judge vs human relevance ratings: Pearson 0.85, Spearman 0.83. Models: Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, o1-mini, o1.
quote: LLMs, including OpenAI's o1, struggle to generate noun phrases which possess given emergent properties
limits: Properties built from ConceptNet and GPT-4o-mini plus crowd filtering; scoring by an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that emergent features are the weak spot of LLM combination. Distant-domain seeds need an external check for emergence.

source: Song et al. (2025): property-type classification and spread-activation method
finding: GPT-4o can tell whether a phrase has a property but is poor at naming the property type. An iterative spread-activation retrieval method helps a little.
numbers: GPT-4o: 95.6% accuracy when the combination has a property, 69.6% when it does not (mean 82.6%). Property type prediction 56.4% vs human 81%. Spread activation over 1 to 5 iterations: emergent property induction 45.1 to 45.8, canceled 60.5 to 63.3. Filter ablation: +1.2 emergent, +7.7 canceled.
limits: Emergent gains are about the size of the reported error (SEM up to 1.7). Metrics rely on an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of related concepts helps cancellation more than emergence. Do not count on it to produce novelty.

source: Ross, Davidson and Kim (2024) Is artificial intelligence still intelligence? LLMs and novel adjective-noun pairs (arXiv 2410.17482)
finding: The largest LLMs draw human-like membership inferences ('is a fake X still an X?') when context decides, and handle zero-frequency bigrams as well as known ones. Without context they match the human spread for at most 75% of items.
numbers: 798 bigrams. Log-probability distributions human-like (JS divergence under 0.25) for 75.3%; generated-context method 61.4%. JS divergence: Llama 3 70B Instruct 0.17 overall (0.26 privative, 0.08 subsective); uniform baseline 0.34; majority baseline 0.40; Llama 2 7B Chat 0.38. Regression on human SD and frequency: R2 0.44 (log-prob) and 0.55 (context).
quote: LLMs show a human-like distribution on at most 75% of our dataset
limits: Adjective-noun, not noun-noun. Only the 70B-class models do well; the within-1-SD metric is a low bar and the majority baseline is high.
agent_relevance: Models generalise to unseen combinations rather than recall them. But they are too confident compared with the spread of human answers, so one sample is not a population.

source: Ross et al. (2024): analogy baseline and size scaling
finding: A GloVe nearest-bigram analogy baseline does worse than larger LLMs, so models do more than copy similar known pairs. Accuracy rises with model size.
numbers: Accuracy on the context-based inference task increases with size; models perform similarly or better on zero-frequency than on high-frequency bigrams. Instruction-tuned models gave a higher, more confident rating than humans for 'artificial intelligence is still intelligence'.
limits: Compared with a low-bar metric. Llama 3 had a bias toward one rating (69.2%) in one probe.
agent_relevance: Size and tuning matter. A small model is a weak combiner; tuned models sound surer than people.

source: Coil and Shwartz (2023) From chocolate bunny to chocolate crocodile (arXiv 2305.10568)
finding: GPT-3 paraphrases familiar noun compounds almost perfectly and novel or rare ones better than crowd workers.
numbers: Human-judged percent correct: GPT-3 95.64% on interpretation of familiar compounds (NCI); on the novel/rare set (NCC) GPT-3 83.81% vs human 73.33%. NCC set drawn from the 500 least frequent compounds in C4, cleaned by hand.
quote: While GPT-3's performance is not perfect, it is better than that of humans
limits: Human baseline from crowd workers with little incentive; authors say effort matters. GPT-3 few-shot.
agent_relevance: Interpreting a given pair is not the bottleneck for a model. Limits are in emergence and in judging.

source: Coil and Shwartz (2023): parroting analysis
finding: GPT-3 output overlaps often with web text, but copying helps less for novel compounds.
numbers: Of n-grams copied from the web, 97% sat in correct NCI paraphrases but only 80% in correct NCC paraphrases. For NCC, correct paraphrases tend to use n-grams that do not appear on the web at all.
limits: Overlap measured against a web corpus (C4), not the true training data.
agent_relevance: Novel pairs need reasoning, not recall. Test the agent on fresh pairs the model cannot have seen.

source: Kumar, Ghosh, Tyagi and Manocha (2024) Do vision-language models understand compound nouns? (Compun, arXiv 2404.00419)
finding: CLIP-style models are weak on compound nouns; reversing the order of the nouns cuts performance sharply; example captions help.
numbers: Compun: 400 unique compounds. Text-to-image selection accuracy (%): human 96.25; CLIP 78.25; OpenCLIP 83.90; MetaCLIP 81.35; CLIP with descriptions 81.15; CLIP with example captions (their method) 86.50 (+8.25); OpenCLIP with examples 86.25 (+2.35); CLIP with nouns reversed 41.00.
limits: Image retrieval, not text generation; distractor images are of the single nouns.
agent_relevance: Noun order is a real variable. Treat head-modifier order as separate candidates.

source: Kendrick, Ormerod, Wang and Devereux (2025) Noun-noun compound relation representations in autoregressive LLMs (CMCL 2025)
finding: Autoregressive models (GPT-2, Phi-1, LLaMA-3.2, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) hold relation information, most strongly at the last token of the compound.
numbers: Representational similarity analysis and probes against 18-dimensional relation vectors, with BERT-Japanese as control. Phi-1 and LLaMA-3.2 predict relation vectors from separate words about as well as from the compound; GPT-2 and DeepSeek-R1 differ between together and separate processing. Exact correlations are in figures and were not read.
limits: Small models only. Probing does not show the model uses the relation when it generates.
agent_relevance: An explicit relation slot in a prompt is plausible, but this is not evidence of better output.

source: Hampton (1987, 1988) composite prototype model, as described in Hampton (2013) and Hampton (1996)
finding: Composite prototype: take the union of constituent attributes, weight by averages, then apply a necessity constraint and coherence repair. It predicts overextension and inheritance failure.
numbers: Examples: chess is a typical game but not a sport, yet most place it in 'sport that is a game'. 'Birds which are pets': migration not inherited; talks and lives in cages are true of the conjunction but of neither part.
limits: Second-hand description. The 1987 and 1988 papers were not opened. Wisniewski and Gentner (1991) argue it misses structure mapping.
agent_relevance: Gives a procedure the agent could run in code: union, weight, drop impossible features, repair.

source: Wisniewski (1997) When concepts combine (PB&R 4:167): comparison and construction
finding: Seen only as a search snippet: adds comparison and construction processes to explain how concepts change when combined, including nominal metaphors. Full text not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Springer redirected to login; the mirror returned HTML, not a PDF.
agent_relevance: Read before citing; it is the source of the hybridization and construction ideas.

source: Costello and Keane (2000) Efficient creativity: constraint-guided conceptual combination (C3 model)
finding: Not opened (Wiley returned 403). Known only from citation lists: constraint satisfaction over diagnosticity, plausibility and informativeness.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not verified this session. No failed replication found.
agent_relevance: Candidate scoring rules for merged candidates; must be read before use.

source: Gagne and Shoben (1997) relation availability (CARIN) and Estes and Glucksberg (2000) interactive property attribution
finding: Not opened. Only a search listing of later relation-availability work (2004, 64 citations) was seen.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not verified this session. Search quota ran out before these could be reached.
agent_relevance: Relation-competition accounts are the main rival to the dual-process view. Still to read.
